title: South Korea's Lee Calls for Talks to End Korean War and Transform Armistice Into Peace
excerpt: In a Liberation Day address, President Lee Jae Myung urged dialogue with North Korea and other parties to replace the 1953 ceasefire with a formal peace regime.
body:
• South Korean President Lee Jae Myung called for talks with North Korea and other parties to formally end the 1950-53 Korean War, which was halted by a ceasefire rather than a peace treaty
  • Lee said the Korean Peninsula's unstable armistice must be transformed into a 'peace regime' and that dialogue could help address North Korea's nuclear capabilities
  • The speech builds on Lee's broader 'peace first' strategy, which prioritizes freezing Pyongyang's nuclear program over demanding immediate denuclearization
  • North Korea has repeatedly rejected Seoul's overtures, with Kim Yo-jong previously dismissing Lee's proposals as a 'pipe dream'

A Push for Peace on Liberation Day

South Korean President Lee Jae Myung used Saturday's anniversary of Korea's liberation from Japanese colonial rule to make his most explicit call yet for talks to formally end the Korean War — a conflict that was halted by a ceasefire in 1953 but never concluded with a peace treaty.

Speaking at the 81st Liberation Day ceremony, Lee said mechanisms must be established to manage tensions with North Korea and called for dialogue involving Pyongyang and other concerned parties, according to Reuters. He argued that the Korean Peninsula's unstable armistice needed to be transformed into what he called a "peace regime."

Building on the 'Peace First' Strategy

The speech represents a continuation and escalation of Lee's diplomatic approach since taking office in June 2025. His government formally shifted South Korea's North Korea policy from "denuclearization first" to "peace first" in July 2026, with Unification Minister Chung Dong-young announcing that Seoul would prioritize an initial freeze of Pyongyang's nuclear program rather than demanding complete disarmament as a precondition for talks.

Lee has previously outlined his vision through the "END" initiative — standing for Exchange, Normalization, and Denuclearization — which he introduced at the United Nations General Assembly in September 2025. The phased approach envisions gradually expanding inter-Korean exchanges to build trust before addressing the nuclear question.

Pyongyang Unmoved

Despite Lee's persistent outreach, North Korea has shown little interest in reciprocating. Pyongyang has said it has no interest in Seoul's proposals or in resuming dialogue, accusing Lee of continuing a confrontational policy through close ties with the United States.

Kim Yo-jong, the powerful sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un, has dismissed the Lee administration's reconciliatory gestures as a "pipe dream." North Korea has made clear it considers its nuclear arsenal non-negotiable and would reject any future talks on denuclearization.

Concrete Steps Already Taken

Lee's government has taken several unilateral steps to ease tensions. Since his inauguration, Seoul has halted the launch of anti-Pyongyang propaganda leaflets and suspended loudspeaker broadcasts directed at the North — measures his predecessor had reinstated. Lee has also signaled interest in restoring the 2018 Comprehensive Military Agreement, which created buffer zones along the border before being suspended in 2024.

At the G7 summit in June 2026, Lee asked U.S. President Donald Trump to lead efforts to resolve the North Korea issue peacefully, drawing a comparison to Washington's engagement in Middle East diplomacy.

What's Next

The Korean War remains one of the longest-running unresolved conflicts in modern history. While Lee's peace proposals face deep skepticism from both Pyongyang and conservative critics at home, his consistent messaging suggests Seoul will continue pressing for dialogue. The question remains whether North Korea, emboldened by its growing nuclear and missile capabilities and deepening ties with Russia, has any incentive to come to the table.
